title: Thyroid Storm
subject: Medicine
summary: Thyroid storm is an acute, life-threatening decompensation of thyrotoxicosis marked by hyperpyrexia, cardiovascular collapse, and altered mental status. It is triggered by physiological stressors in poorly controlled hyperthyroidism. Treatment must start immediately on clinical suspicion without waiting for laboratory confirmation.

sections.p: Thyroid storm is a clinical emergency defined as extreme, organ-threatening decompensation of thyrotoxicosis. Diagnosis is entirely clinical; serum thyroid hormone concentrations do not distinguish uncomplicated thyrotoxicosis from thyroid storm.
b: Clinical diagnosis based on severe hypermetabolism affecting central nervous, cardiovascular, and gastrointestinal systems.
Characterised by high fever, tachycardia out of proportion to fever, neurological dysfunction, and hemodynamic instability.
Do not delay therapy to wait for confirmatory laboratory results.

sections.p: The Burch-Wartofsky Point Scale (BWPS) quantifies clinical severity using points assigned across physiological domains. The Japanese Thyroid Association (JTA) criteria provide an alternative diagnostic system.
b: BWPS score 45 or more: highly suggestive of thyroid storm.
BWPS score 25 to 44: supports impending thyroid storm.
BWPS score below 25: thyroid storm is unlikely.
Scoring domains include thermoregulatory dysfunction, central nervous system effects, gastrointestinal-hepatic dysfunction, cardiovascular dysfunction, and precipitating history.

sections.p: Underlying thyrotoxicosis (most commonly Graves' disease or toxic multinodular goitre) decompensates when an acute physiological stressor sharply shifts hormone binding or triggers massive adrenergic discharge.
b: Infections: severe pneumonia, urinary tract infections, malaria, sepsis, or tuberculosis.
Non-adherence: abrupt cessation of antithyroid medications (carbimazole or propylthiouracil).
Surgical stress: emergency thyroid or non-thyroid surgery without adequate preoperative control.
Acute medical events: diabetic ketoacidosis, myocardial infarction, stroke, or pulmonary embolism.
Obstetric events: labour, delivery, pre-eclampsia, or gestational trophoblastic disease.
Exogenous triggers: radioactive iodine therapy, iodinated radiocontrast agents, or amiodarone.

sections.p: Patients appear profoundly toxic, agitated, flushed, and diaphoretic with evidence of severe multisystem hypermetabolic collapse.
b: Thermoregulatory: marked hyperpyrexia often exceeding 39 degrees Celsius with drenching diaphoresis.
Cardiovascular: severe sinus tachycardia or rapid atrial fibrillation disproportionate to fever, wide pulse pressure, or acute heart failure.
Neurological: severe agitation, emotional lability, delirium, psychosis, seizure, or progressive coma.
Gastrointestinal: nausea, intractable vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, and jaundice indicating hepatic congestion or injury.
Goitre, ophthalmopathy, or pretibial myxedema may reveal the underlying Graves' disease.

t.a: Serum TSH, free T4, free T3
t.b: Confirms thyrotoxicosis (suppressed TSH, elevated free T4/T3); values do not correlate with clinical severity of storm; treat before results return if testing is delayed.
Differentiates from diabetic ketoacidosis or detects stress-induced hyperglycaemia; immediate bedside result directs urgent glycemic support.

t.a: Blood film and rapid diagnostic test for malaria
t.b: Identifies malaria as the acute infectious trigger in endemic tropical settings; directs targeted antimalarial therapy.
Assesses for infectious trigger via leukocytosis; excludes antithyroid drug-induced agranulocytosis if patient was previously on carbimazole.
Identifies sinus tachycardia, atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, ischemic changes, or prolonged QT interval.
Assesses end-organ dysfunction (jaundice, elevated transaminases) and detects dehydration, hypokalaemia, or hypercalcaemia.

t.a: Blood, urine, and sputum cultures; chest radiograph
t.b: Identifies the occult precipitating source of infection triggering the hypermetabolic crisis.

sections.p: Thyroid storm carries a high mortality rate even with aggressive therapy. Death occurs rapidly from progressive shock, arrhythmias, or multi-organ failure.
b: Cardiovascular collapse: high-output heart failure transitioning into low-output cardiogenic shock.
Malignant dysrhythmias: rapid atrial fibrillation, ventricular tachycardia, or cardiovascular collapse.
Neurological deterioration: progression from delirium to status epilepticus or unresponsive coma.
Hepatic failure: acute hepatocellular necrosis and profound coagulopathy.
Relative adrenal insufficiency: hypermetabolic cortisol consumption exhausting adrenal synthetic capacity.

sections.p: Management requires aggressive, sequential pharmacotherapy aimed at blocking peripheral adrenergic drive, synthesising new hormone, releasing stored hormone, and preventing peripheral conversion, alongside treating the underlying trigger.
b: Adrenergic blockade: propranolol is preferred because it controls tachycardia and blocks peripheral conversion of T4 to T3; cardioselective beta-blockers are used if asthma precludes non-selective agents.
Block new hormone synthesis: thionamides (propylthiouracil or carbimazole) administered immediately; propylthiouracil also inhibits peripheral T4 to T3 conversion.
Block hormone release: inorganic iodine (Lugols iodine or potassium iodide) given at least 60 minutes AFTER thionamides to prevent iodine serving as substrate for new synthesis.
Block peripheral conversion and support adrenals: intravenous hydrocortisone or dexamethasone reduces T4 to T3 conversion and treats potential relative adrenal crisis.
Cooling and supportive care: paracetamol and active cooling blankets; avoid aspirin as it displaces thyroid hormone from thyroid-binding globulin.
Resuscitation and trigger treatment: intravenous fluids without dextrose if euglycemic, empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics, or antimalarials if infection is suspected.

sections.p: Once stabilized in an intensive care setting, transition to definitive outpatient endocrine management is mandatory to prevent recurrence.
b: Taper glucocorticoids and inorganic iodine once acute crisis has clinically resolved.
Maintain maintenance thionamide therapy and monitor thyroid function every 4 to 6 weeks.
Counsel on medication adherence and warn regarding the early symptoms of infection and agranulocytosis.
Plan definitive control via radioactive iodine ablation or total thyroidectomy once euthyroid.
Ensure pre-operative euthyroid preparation before any planned elective surgery.

sections.p: Thyroid storm shares features with other hypermetabolic and hyperpyrexic emergencies; physical examination and collateral history are key.
b: Severe sepsis: shares fever, tachycardia, and altered mental status; thyroid storm usually lacks focal suppurative focus and features pronounced goitre or thyrotoxic eye signs.
Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS): presents with hyperthermia and confusion, but distinguished by severe 'lead-pipe' muscle rigidity and antipsychotic use.
Malignant Hyperthermia: acute intraoperative hypermetabolic crisis with jaw spasm and muscle rigidity following volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine.
Sympathomimetic toxicity: cocaine or amphetamine overdose causes hyperadrenergic state; distinguished by toxicological history and lack of previous thyrotoxic symptoms.
Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA): severe metabolic acidosis with tachycardia; DKA can also co-occur as the trigger for storm.

sections.p: Clinicians must recognize situations where laboratory investigations and clinical measurements mask or mimic thyroid storm.
b: Serum thyroid hormone values: free T4 and T3 are elevated in both storm and uncomplicated hyperthyroidism; magnitude does not define storm.
Apathetic thyrotoxicosis: elderly patients may present with lethargy, depression, and heart failure without dramatic agitation or fever.
Serum bilirubin: isolated elevation can reflect passive congestive hepatopathy from high-output failure rather than primary liver failure.
Non-thyroidal illness syndrome: critically ill septic patients can have abnormal thyroid tests with low TSH, but free hormones are usually low or normal.

whenToSeekHelp: Unexplained high fever (above 38.5 degrees Celsius) with resting heart rate over 120 beats per minute.
New-onset severe agitation, disorientation, hallucination, or sudden lethargy.
Shortness of breath with leg swelling or chest pain in a patient with a goitre.
Persistent vomiting, severe diarrhoea, or new yellowish discolouration of the eyes.

faq.q: Why must inorganic iodine be delayed until after the thionamide is given?
faq.a: Giving iodine first provides a substrate for new thyroid hormone synthesis (the Jod-Basedow effect). Thionamides must block organification for at least one hour before iodine is given to safely halt hormone release.

faq.q: Why is aspirin avoided to lower fever in thyroid storm?
faq.a: Aspirin displaces thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3) from thyroid-binding globulin, increasing the concentration of free, biologically active thyroid hormone and worsening toxicity. Paracetamol is the antipyretic of choice.

faq.q: Can thyroid storm occur with normal free T4 levels?
faq.a: Rarely, isolated T3 thyrotoxicosis (elevated free T3 with normal free T4) can decompensate into thyroid storm. Clinical diagnosis remains paramount regardless of specific hormone fraction values.

exam: A 32-year-old woman with a goitre presents with fever of 39.8°C, pulse of 150, and severe delirium; what is your immediate first step? — Recognize clinical thyroid storm, initiate airway protection and IV access, start beta-blockade and thionamides immediately, and do not delay treatment for lab confirmation.

Why must you administer propylthiouracil or carbimazole before potassium iodide? — Administering iodine before blocking thyroid peroxidase allows the thyroid to use iodine as a substrate to synthesize more hormone; thionamides block organification first.

An intern orders aspirin to control the temperature of 40°C in suspected thyroid storm. Why do you intervene? — Aspirin displaces T4 and T3 from thyroid-binding proteins, raising free hormone levels and worsening hypermetabolism; use paracetamol and physical cooling instead.

How does the Burch-Wartofsky Point Scale guide clinical decision-making? — It systematically scores fever, CNS agitation, tachycardia, heart failure, and GI symptoms; a score of 45 or more strongly supports storm, prompting empirical emergency therapy.

A patient with known thyrotoxicosis presents in storm with fever and sore throat. What medication side effect must you urgently exclude? — Thionamide-induced agranulocytosis; obtain an immediate full blood count with differential and blood cultures before prescribing further antithyroid drugs.

Why are systemic corticosteroids included in the emergency management protocol for thyroid storm? — Glucocorticoids inhibit the peripheral conversion of T4 to T3 and treat potential relative adrenal insufficiency caused by accelerated cortisol metabolism.

What signs distinguish thyroid storm from severe cerebral malaria in an East African emergency unit? — Both cause high fever and altered mental status, but thyroid storm demonstrates pronounced thyrotoxic eye signs, goitre, marked tremor, and extreme sinus tachycardia out of proportion to fever; thick and thin blood films confirm or exclude malaria.
